title: Have We Reached 'Peak Legal Tech?' Sure Felt That Way At ILTACON this Week
author: Bob Ambrogi

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: Ambrogi offers a market-level snapshot of rapid integrations, vendor volatility and unequal purchasing capacity. This partially aligns with selective, workflow-embedded deployment, but the source does not assess task-level capability, general legal competence, verification or human–AI work redesign sufficiently to establish a position on the cluster’s principal proposition.
qs: The other is the desire by vendors to meet lawyers where they work.
They are having to make hard choices about which products to invest in.

kp.k: Record conference scale signals legal technology industry momentum
kp.d: Ambrogi reports that ILTACON registrations reached 5,700 by Wednesday, compared with 4,600 the previous year, with further registrations expected. The conference featured 241 exhibit booths, three times the previous year's shipped booth-and-equipment tonnage, and attendees from 29 countries. These are conference-scale indicators underlying the article's discussion of industry excitement, rather than measurements of AI adoption or legal productivity.
qs: As of Wednesday, registrations had reached 5,700, 1,100 more than last year’s 4,600, and ILTA expected that number to go even higher before the week was over.
The 241 booths in the exhibit hall beat last year’s number, but the bigger story was the size and ostentatiousness of some of the booths.
Compared to last year, the sheer tonnage of booths and related equipment shipped into the exhibit hall was three times more than last year.

kp.k: Well-funded AI vendors display conspicuous spending
kp.d: Ambrogi connects Harvey's and Legora's fundraising and billion-dollar valuations with large booths and celebrity entertainment. His explicitly uncertain initial booth estimates differ from a parenthetical report attributed to Haydn Jones: Harvey and Fulcrum each occupied 24 10×10 spaces, Legora 22, and Clio 18, with spaces priced at $10,000 before applicable discounts. The article reports attendee criticism of spending but does not establish actual total event expenditures.
qs: If you did not know that Harvey and Legora had raised tons of money and achieved valuations in the billions of dollars, their parties might have clued you in.
Both had big-name celebrities as performers – Lady A at Harvey’s party and Sheryl Crow at Legora’s party.
The big booths and the big parties had some attendees bemoaning the obscenity of such over-the-top and unnecessary spending.

kp.k: Enterprise technology funding contrasts with access-to-justice scarcity
kp.d: Ambrogi argues that lavish enterprise legal-tech spending exposes a funding imbalance between technology serving large firms and corporate legal departments and technology addressing low-income Americans' unmet legal needs. Reprising his 2024 comparison of Legalweek and the Legal Services Corporation's Innovations in Technology Conference, he suggests that contributions from the better-funded sector could modestly narrow the justice gap. This is a normative argument, not a quantified funding study.
qs: the gaping funding gap between those who are developing technology to better meet the legal needs of low-income Americans and those who are developing legal tech to serve large law firms and corporate legal departments.

When some legal tech companies have so much money that they do not know what to do with it, and other legal tech companies are struggling to raise capital to help needy individuals get access to legal help and legal resources, then this industry is horribly out of kilter.

If the legal tech sector reflected at Legalweek contributed more to the sector reflected at ITC, perhaps that imbalance could be offset, at least slightly, and the justice gap narrowed, even just a bit.

kp.k: Partnerships integrate AI with data and lawyers' workflows
kp.d: Ambrogi identifies partnerships and integrations, including MCP and APIs, as a central vendor theme. He attributes this to demand for better AI inputs and a desire to operate where lawyers already work, reporting frequent references to Anthropic's Claude CoWork. Thomson Reuters executives said their ecosystem graphic would become outdated within months or weeks; this conveys their expectation of rapid change rather than demonstrated integration outcomes.
qs: If there was a theme among the products and vendors this year, it was partnerships and integrations.
Suddenly, it seems, everyone is friends with everyone else, and everyone is MCP-ing, API-ing, or otherwise integrating with everyone else.
One is the need for better data to drive better AI. The other is the desire by vendors to meet lawyers where they work.
An interesting theme at ILTACON was how often the answer to that “where they work” question turned out to be Anthropic’s Claude CoWork.

kp.k: Hiring may explain perceived younger conference attendance
kp.d: Ambrogi perceives a younger attendee population but explicitly acknowledges having no supporting numbers. Conditional on that perception being correct, he attributes it partly to hiring during the previous year by Harvey, Legora and other growing companies, alongside law firms expanding innovation and IT teams. This is an observational hypothesis, not demographic or employment evidence.
qs: It also felt as if ILTACON’s attendees skewed distinctly younger this year. I have no numbers to back that up, but I know I was not alone in sensing that.
Assuming I am correct in that perception, I attribute it, at least in part, to the hiring that is going on.

Think of all the people hired in the last year just by Harvey and Legora, and then look across so many fast-growing companies, not to mention law firms rapidly expanding their innovation and IT staffs.

kp.k: Large firms hedge vendor risk through multiple purchases
kp.d: Based on what he hears rather than a specified survey, Ambrogi reports that many large firms buy Harvey, Legora and CoCounsel together to retain alternatives if a product fails. He contrasts this with mid-sized and smaller firms, which he says cannot afford comparable hedging and must make consequential product choices amid increasing market volatility.
qs: From what I hear, many large firms are hedging their bets.
They are not buying Harvey instead of Legora, or Legora instead of CoCounsel. They are buying them all. If one fails, they still have another.
Unfortunately, mid-sized and smaller firms do not have the luxury of hedging their bets across product groups.
As the market grows more volatile, those choices will be either prescient or disastrous.

kp.k: Author predicts market realignment rather than imminent collapse
kp.d: Despite describing unusually high excitement and uncertainty, Ambrogi does not expect a bubble burst before the following year's ILTACON and believes the ultimate peak remains ahead. He predicts correction and normalization through vendor failures, successes and acquisitions, with entrants continuing to outnumber departures. His stated rationale for continued industry growth is the legal profession's durability and ongoing need for technology; these are forecasts, not established outcomes.
qs: Yes, there has never been a more exciting time in legal tech. But there has also never been a more uncertain one.
I, for one, do not think the bubble will burst between this year’s ILTACON and next year’s.
More likely than a burst, I think, is a realignment, a correction, a normalization.
Vendors will come and go. Some will thrive, some will fail, and some will be gobbled up by others.

But more will keep coming than will be going, and legal tech, as an industry, will continue to grow, because the legal profession is durable and essential and is not going anywhere, and legal professionals will continue to need the tools and capabilities that legal tech provides.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: Ambrogi describes an expanding but unevenly funded legal-tech market, with AI driving integrations, hiring and differentiated purchasing strategies; he predicts correction and consolidation rather than an imminent collapse.
pts.d: Ambrogi identifies partnerships and integrations as the conference's main product trend, attributing them to the need for better data for AI and vendors' desire to integrate into lawyers' existing work environments, frequently Claude CoWork. He argues that funding is disproportionately concentrated in technology serving large firms and corporate legal departments rather than low-income individuals; greater contributions from the well-funded sector could modestly narrow the justice gap. He tentatively links a perceived younger conference audience to hiring by Harvey, Legora and other growing companies, alongside expanding law-firm innovation and IT teams. He reports that many large firms buy multiple competing AI products to hedge vendor risk, whereas smaller firms must make selective investments. His market forecast is continued growth accompanied by vendor failures, acquisitions and realignment, not a bubble burst before the next ILTACON. These are primarily claims about vendors, adoption and market structure, rather than measured changes in legal-work quality or productivity.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The source relies on conference statistics, firsthand observation, vendor briefings and informal conversations; its hiring explanation and market outlook are explicitly interpretive.
pts.d: Ambrogi supports the picture of market activity with reported registrations of 5,700 versus 4,600 the previous year, 241 exhibit booths, and three times the prior year's shipped booth-and-equipment tonnage. Spending observations include large booths and celebrity parties by AI vendors. These describe conference scale and expenditure, not demonstrated AI performance or legal-service outcomes. His integration account draws on conference encounters and a Thomson Reuters briefing graphic; Thomson Reuters executives, rather than Ambrogi alone, say that graphic will soon become outdated. His funding-gap argument also references his own 2024 comparison of enterprise legal-tech and access-to-justice conferences. Multi-product purchasing is attributed to what he hears, without survey data. He expressly has no demographic figures supporting the younger-attendee impression and offers no quantified hiring evidence. The prediction of continued growth rests on his judgment that legal services remain essential, not on a presented market model.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: Observations concern the ILTACON reported in August 2026; the no-burst forecast extends to the following year's conference, while continued growth has no specified endpoint.
pts.d: The integration, spending and purchasing claims describe current conditions at the conference. Thomson Reuters executives anticipate changes to their integration graphic within months or weeks. Ambrogi refers to hiring during the preceding year and conditions his demographic explanation on the accuracy of an unmeasured impression. The proposed justice-gap benefit is explicitly conditional and modest: contributions from enterprise-focused legal tech might offset the imbalance slightly. He does not rule out volatility, failures or acquisitions; instead, he predicts no bubble burst between this conference and the next and argues that the ultimate peak remains ahead. His longer-term growth forecast assumes durable demand from the legal profession, without a quantified growth rate or deadline.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The claimed effects differ across enterprise buyers, smaller firms, vendors, technology staff and people with unmet legal needs.
pts.d: Large law firms can spread risk across Harvey, Legora and CoCounsel subscriptions; mid-sized and smaller firms lack that purchasing flexibility and face greater consequences from choosing particular products. Lawyers are the intended beneficiaries of integrations bringing AI into their existing work environments. AI vendors and other legal-tech companies face growth opportunities alongside failure and acquisition risk. Hiring is described at AI companies and in law-firm innovation and IT functions, not as evidence of changes to associate staffing or lawyer displacement. Large firms and corporate legal departments are the well-funded technology market's customers, while developers serving low-income Americans struggle to raise capital. The corresponding access-to-justice concern is unmet individual legal need, distinct from enterprise technology savings.
